questions.prompt: What is the first step when a housemate says Milo is 'acting strange'?

options.text: Choose the most likely explanation before the details become confusing.
options.feedback: An early explanation can hide the observation. The method begins with Milo's personal baseline and a specific account of what differs.

options.text: Return to the recorded baseline and specify frequency, intensity, duration, a new behaviour, or a missing usual one.
options.feedback: This is the best answer because it converts an impression into a comparison that can be checked again and communicated clearly.

options.text: Compare Milo with an average cat of the same age rather than with her own history.
options.feedback: General expectations can inform context, but this method is built around what is normal for this individual cat.

questions.prompt: Why does the method check urgent signatures before testing a benign explanation?

options.text: A plausible household change must not delay help for an already recognised time-sensitive pattern.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. An urgent signature changes the action even when a visitor, schedule shift, or other story appears to fit.

options.text: Every changed behaviour is urgent until a veterinarian proves otherwise.
options.feedback: That collapses the method into over-escalation. Urgency depends on the observed pattern, not the mere existence of variation.

options.text: Household explanations are never useful because only clinical causes affect behaviour.
options.feedback: Environmental explanations can be useful when timing fits and the behaviour resolves, but they come after the urgent-pattern check.

options.text: A gradual real change is absorbed into memory until the household says Milo has always been that way.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Dated comparisons protect against familiarity quietly moving the definition of normal.

options.text: A harmless one-day variation is documented without arranging an emergency visit.
options.feedback: Proportionate observation is not drift. Drift occurs when a sustained change disappears from judgement because the baseline shifts with it.

options.text: A veterinarian updates clinical guidance as new research becomes available.
options.feedback: That may be appropriate revision, but it is unrelated to the course's named failure mode in personal baseline comparison.

questions.prompt: When does a non-urgent change belong in a veterinary conversation?

options.text: Only when it becomes dramatic enough that every housemate agrees.
options.feedback: Waiting for drama invites normalisation drift. A persistent or worsening unexplained change can matter before it becomes visually striking.

options.text: When no benign explanation fits, or the change persists or worsens instead of resolving.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. It distinguishes immediate emergency action from a prompt professional conversation and from explained observation.

options.text: Never, unless it matches the exact obstruction signature learned in Chapter 3.
options.feedback: That signature requires immediate escalation, but it is not the only reason to contact a vet. Persistent unexplained change also deserves discussion.

questions.prompt: Milo scratches more during a houseguest's stay and returns to baseline after the guest leaves. No urgent sign appears. What is the best response?

options.text: Log the timed, explained, resolved change and continue ordinary observation.
options.feedback: This is the best response because all four steps were completed and the return to baseline supports the proposed explanation.

options.text: Erase it from the log because explained behaviour cannot inform future care.
options.feedback: The event shows how Milo responds to disruption and may improve future preparation. Explained does not mean irrelevant.

options.text: Treat the two-week duration as an emergency even after the pattern resolves.
options.feedback: Duration should be recorded, but this case lacks an urgent signature and includes a fitting cause plus documented resolution.

questions.prompt: Two housemates disagree about Milo's appetite, but only one has kept notes. What is the safest use of the method?

options.text: Accept the note-keeper's interpretation because written records make their causal explanation correct.
options.feedback: The notes may strengthen the observation, but they do not automatically prove its cause. Observation and interpretation remain separate.

options.text: Reconstruct the supported baseline from notes and both accounts, state the gap, and use lower confidence going forward.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Incomplete data changes confidence; it does not justify either certainty or abandonment of the method.

options.text: Average the two memories and treat the midpoint as Milo's objective baseline.
options.feedback: Memories are not numerical measurements, and averaging incompatible accounts hides rather than resolves the evidence gap.

questions.prompt: Milo drinks more for a week, there is no household explanation, and no known emergency signature appears. Which conclusion best balances the two failure modes?

options.text: Keep waiting because the absence of an emergency proves the change is harmless.
options.feedback: This confuses non-urgent with insignificant and risks normalisation drift when an unexplained pattern persists.

options.text: Record the specific trend and raise it with the vet, without claiming a diagnosis or treating it as an emergency by default.
options.feedback: This is the best synthesis: it neither explains away the persistent change nor inflates it beyond the evidence.

options.text: Select the most likely disease online so the vet conversation starts with a firm diagnosis.
options.feedback: The owner-level method supports observation and escalation, not diagnosis. A guessed disease adds certainty the available evidence cannot carry.
